The Museum of Almost occupied a narrow building between a bank and a shop that sold only buttons. Above its door, brass letters had loosened with age, so some evenings the sign read MUSEUM OF MOST. Inside were a ticket for a ship that had sailed without its owner, a wedding ring never offered, eleven unsent letters, and a violin with one string tuned for a song nobody had finished. Admission was free. Visitors usually entered laughing and left speaking softly, as though the building were a hospital for patients whose illnesses had names no doctor could ever fully recognize.

Elias Venn, the curator, had worked there for over thirty years. He dusted the exhibits each morning, polished their small white labels, and recorded new donations in a green ledger. He preferred unfinished things to completed ones. A finished symphony could disappoint; an unfinished symphony remained infinite. A rejected proposal acquired a story, while an unspoken proposal kept every possible answer. This was what he told schoolchildren, donors, and journalists. It was also what he told himself whenever he locked the museum at dusk and returned, alone, to the flat above the button shop with its narrow view of chimneys.

One October afternoon, a young woman entered carrying a key on a length of red string. Rain jeweled her coat. She set the key beside Elias’s ledger and said she wished to donate the apartment it had once opened. The apartment was in another city, small and bright, with a window facing east. She had rented it at age twenty, packed two suitcases, and bought a houseplant. Then her mother became ill. She stayed. The plant died; the key remained. For twelve years, she had used it to open nothing except the same decision every single morning before leaving home.

Elias touched the key but did not take it. Donations required a label, and labels required an ending. He asked what had happened to her mother. She said her mother had died in spring, gently, after asking for windows and apricots. He asked about the apartment. The young woman laughed once, without much humor. Someone else lived there now. Still, she had kept the key because returning it had seemed like admitting that staying had been a choice. Sometimes, she said, duty and fear wear the same coat, and you notice only when one of them finally takes it off.

She looked around at the hushed glass cases. What, she asked, was the museum for, if not admission? Elias had no answer ready. Usually visitors wanted their almosts preserved, not examined. The young woman wound the red string around her finger, then unwound it. At last she slipped the key into her pocket. Perhaps she would mail it back. Perhaps she would throw it into the river. Perhaps she would try every lock she passed until someone shouted. She smiled at this, and Elias saw her leave before she moved. Not the building, but the whole life waiting beyond it.

After she had gone, the museum seemed incorrectly arranged. The unsent letters looked less patient than cowardly. The violin appeared to be holding its breath. Elias climbed the narrow stairs to his office and opened the bottom drawer, beneath catalogues, twine, and a tin of buttons donated by a woman who had almost become a tailor. There lay his own exhibit: a blue train ticket, unused, its corners soft as cloth. On the back, in green ink, Leila had written, “Come before you understand why not.” He had spent over twenty years considering the question until it became an answer.

He remembered Leila standing on the platform with paint on her wrist, furious and hopeful. She had been offered a studio by the sea. He had promised to follow after one more season, when the museum’s roof was mended, when the ledger was balanced, when certainty arrived wearing clean shoes. Certainty had never come. Leila’s letters had continued for a while, then stopped. Elias did not imagine she was waiting. People who wait become statues in the stories of those who leave them; actual people buy groceries, forgive strangers, and change. Their lives do not hold our places open indefinitely.

At six, Elias turned the sign in the museum door. Instead of CLOSED, he wrote on the back, GONE TO FIND OUT. The sentence pleased and embarrassed him. He put on his coat, then removed it because the buttons frightened him with their usefulness. Then he telephoned the railway. Yes, a clerk said, trains still left for the coast. No, the old blue tickets were not valid. Elias looked at his ticket and felt an almost rise, sleek and reasonable: almost went, almost asked, almost began. He hated it so purely that he laughed, and all the cases laughed back.

He left the ticket on the counter, beside the green ledger, and walked toward the station with his suitcase. The button seller, closing her shop, asked whether the museum had finally been robbed. Yes, Elias said. By the curator. She gave him a paper bag of sandwiches and a small brass button for luck, though luck, she admitted, was mostly what people called a door after somebody else had opened it. At the station, he bought a new ticket. On the platform, he did not think of Leila. He thought of the sea, which he had never bothered to see.

The train arrived with its ordinary thunder. Elias boarded, found a window, and ate a sandwich as the town loosened into fields. Behind him, the museum kept its hundred perfect possibilities. The ring would never be refused. The letters would never be opened. The ship would forever be about to sail. Ahead lay no preserved horizon, only weather, expense, wrong turns, and the likelihood of arriving too late for something. Elias pressed the brass button into his palm. When dawn came, it did not promise anything. It simply made the window bright enough to show his face, then the sea.
